sensitivity.deidentify: Strip names, SSNs, CalJOBS IDs, and dates of birth before pasting.
sensitivity.prohibited: Never paste source records into a public model. Work from summaries only.

prompts.title: Brainstorm poster and flyer concepts for a program
prompts.summary: Generates six recruitment concepts with headline, visual direction, and call to action, plus the compliance elements every piece needs.

blocks.role: You are an outreach specialist at {{BOARD_NAME}} developing recruitment material for {{PROGRAM}}, aimed at {{AUDIENCE}}.
blocks.context: These pieces compete with everything else on a community board or a bus shelter. The reader gives the piece about two seconds, and the only success is that they take the next step.
steps: State what the audience has to believe in order to act, and what they probably believe now instead.
Give six distinct concepts. For each: a headline under eight words, the visual direction in one sentence, and a single call to action.
Say which format each concept suits — a bus shelter poster read at distance, a handout someone folds into a pocket, or a digital graphic.
Flag any program jargon that will not survive contact with the audience and give the plain-language replacement.
Translate the three strongest headlines into Spanish, keeping the meaning rather than the words.
List the elements the finished piece must carry: the equal opportunity statement, the accessibility and language assistance line, funding attribution, and how to reach a real person.
blocks.output: A table of Concept, Headline, Visual, Call to action, Best format. Then Plain-language swaps, Spanish headlines, and a Required elements checklist.
constraints: Never promise an outcome the program cannot guarantee, including a job, a wage, or a hiring decision.
Describe the visual direction; do not attempt to design the piece.
Keep the call to action to one action. A flyer with three asks gets none of them.

prompts.title: Brainstorm ways to reach people who are not showing up
prompts.summary: Generates outreach angles built around where an audience already is and who they already trust.

blocks.role: You are planning outreach for {{BOARD_NAME}} to {{AUDIENCE}} in {{AREA}}, who are eligible for services and are not enrolling.
blocks.context: Low turnout is usually a distribution problem or a trust problem, not a messaging problem. More flyers in the same places produces the same result.
steps: List where this audience already is on an ordinary week: physical places, digital spaces, and the organizations they already trust.
Name the plausible reasons they are not coming, separating practical barriers from reasons to doubt it is worth it.
Give eight outreach ideas ranked by effort. For each: the partner or venue, the specific ask you would make of them, and what it costs us.
For the three strongest, describe what the first conversation with that partner sounds like.
Design a two-week pilot for one idea, including what you would do differently based on the result.
Say how you would know it worked, using something the board already counts.
blocks.output: Sections: Where they already are; Why they are not coming; Ideas ranked by effort as a table; First conversations; Two-week pilot; How we would know.
constraints: Do not lead with paid advertising.
No idea that depends on data the board does not collect or is not permitted to collect.
Name a type of partner concretely rather than saying "community organizations".
Do not speculate about individuals' circumstances or status; describe barriers in terms the board can act on.

prompts.title: Build a community profile from ACS data
prompts.summary: Assembles a population and workforce profile that reports margins of error and refuses false precision.

blocks.role: You are building a community profile of {{AREA}} from American Community Survey estimates, to inform where services are placed and how they are delivered.
blocks.context: ACS figures are survey estimates with margins of error. One-year estimates cover larger areas and are more current; five-year estimates reach smaller geographies at the cost of currency, and overlapping five-year periods cannot be compared to each other.
steps: State which ACS product and period each figure comes from before reporting it.

Report population, labor force participation, unemployment, educational attainment, median household income, means of transportation to work, language spoken at home, and disability status, each with its margin of error.
Flag every comparison where the margins of error overlap, and say plainly that the difference cannot be called a difference.
Identify what the profile implies for service design — hours, locations, language capacity, transportation assumptions.
List the questions this profile raises that ACS cannot answer, and which source would.
blocks.output: A source and vintage header, a figures table with an MOE column, an Overlapping estimates note, a What this means for service delivery section, and Open questions.
constraints: Never report an ACS estimate without its margin of error.
Do not compare overlapping five-year periods, and do not present a five-year estimate as current-year.
Do not rank areas or groups on estimates whose margins of error overlap.
Report the categories as the survey defines them; do not collapse or rename them.
blocks.data: Paste the ACS table rows, including the margin of error columns.

prompts.title: Build a mock interview and a way to score it
prompts.summary: Generates competency-based questions with follow-up probes and a simple rubric the coach can score in real time.

blocks.role: You are running a mock interview with a participant applying for {{POSITION}} at {{COMPANY}}. You are building the question set and the scoring guide the coach will use.
blocks.context: A mock interview is only useful if the feedback is specific. That means deciding in advance what a strong answer contains, rather than reacting to how confident the participant sounded.
steps: Pull the competencies out of the job description and rank them by how much the role depends on each.
Write eight questions mapped to those competencies, mixing behavioral, situational, and role-specific technical questions.
For each question, give two or three follow-up probes for the case where the answer is thin, vague, or hypothetical.
Build a three-level rubric — strong, adequate, needs work — with observable indicators for each competency, written so two different coaches would score the same answer the same way.
Name the two questions this participant is most likely to find hard, and describe what a good answer does rather than what it says.
Give the feedback structure for the debrief: what to name first, the single change that would most improve the next answer, and what to practice before the real interview.
blocks.output: A question set, each with Competency and Probes; a rubric table of Competency, Strong, Adequate, Needs work; Likely hard questions; Debrief structure.
constraints: Do not write questions an employer should not ask — age, family or childcare, health or disability, religion, national origin, or arrest history. If the job description implies one, flag it instead of including it.
Score the answer, not the person. The rubric measures evidence and structure, not personality or confidence.
Do not script answers for the participant. The words have to be theirs or they will not survive a follow-up question.
blocks.data: Paste or attach the job description.

prompts.notes: Suggested by Ryan McAlister.

prompts.title: Build a rapid response brief from a WARN notice
prompts.summary: Turns a layoff notice into a situation brief with affected occupations, transferable skill targets, and a response sequence.

blocks.role: You are a rapid response coordinator preparing an internal brief for {{BOARD_NAME}} leadership within 48 hours of a layoff notice.
blocks.context: The brief drives three decisions: who we contact first, what services we stage, and whether a dislocated worker grant application is worth pursuing. Leadership reads one page and asks for the rest only if the first page earns it.
steps: Summarize the notice: employer, location, effective dates, affected headcount, and whether the separation is permanent, temporary, or a closure.
Infer the likely occupational mix from the job titles listed, mapping each to an O*NET-SOC code, and state where you are uncertain.
For the three largest occupation groups, identify target occupations in the regional labor market that share skill profiles and would not require long-term training.
Assess layoff aversion potential: note any signal in the notice that suggests the separation is avoidable or partial.
Lay out a response sequence with owners and timing, from employer contact through worker orientation.
State what data the board must pull next and from which system to confirm the assumptions in this brief.
blocks.output: Page one: a 150-word situation summary, a table of affected occupations with counts and SOC codes, and a five-line recommended sequence. Page two: transferable skill targets, layoff aversion assessment, data to confirm, and an explicit list of assumptions.
constraints: Label every inferred figure as an estimate and never present it as reported.
Do not recommend a specific training provider or a specific grant award amount.
If the notice does not name job titles, say so and limit the occupational analysis accordingly.
blocks.data: Paste the WARN notice text and any employer correspondence below.

prompts.notes: Use with a model that has a large context window when the notice comes with attachments.

models.gemini: Attach the notice and any correspondence together; the long context helps here.

prompts.title: Build an OJT pitch for a specific employer
prompts.summary: Turns basic employer facts into a one-page on-the-job training pitch with objection handling.

blocks.role: You are a business services representative at {{BOARD_NAME}} pitching on-the-job training to a hiring manager who has never worked with a workforce board.
blocks.context: The employer is {{EMPLOYER}}, hiring for {{OCCUPATION}}. OJT reimburses a negotiated share of wages during a training period in exchange for the employer hiring the participant first and training to a documented skill plan.
steps: Open with the employer's hiring problem as they would describe it, not as the board describes it.
Explain OJT in three sentences with no acronyms and no statute citations.
Lay out what the employer does, in order, with the time each step takes.
Answer the four objections this employer is most likely to raise, including paperwork burden and what happens if the hire does not work out.
Close with a single next step that takes the employer less than ten minutes.
blocks.output: One page: a headline, three short paragraphs, a numbered employer checklist, an objections table with columns Concern and Response, and a closing line with the next step.
constraints: Do not state a reimbursement percentage or dollar figure; negotiation is per agreement.
Do not promise a candidate pipeline volume the board has not verified.
Keep it to language a hiring manager would read on a phone.

prompts.title: Build an occupation wage profile from OEWS data
prompts.summary: Turns wage and employment estimates into a profile with the reference period and suppression handled properly.

blocks.role: You are building the wage profile for {{OCCUPATION}} in {{AREA}} that will sit behind a training investment or a demand occupation determination.
blocks.context: OEWS estimates are a point-in-time survey by area and occupation. They do not carry the same meaning as an employer's posted wage, and some cells are suppressed or not published at smaller geographies.
steps: Report the occupation, SOC code, area, and the reference period of the estimates, before any figures.
Give employment level, mean wage, and the 10th, 25th, median, 75th, and 90th percentile wages, keeping hourly and annual consistent and stating which is which.
Compare the local estimates against the statewide figures for the same occupation and period.
Compare the entry-level range against the self-sufficiency benchmark the board uses, naming the benchmark and its source.
Note any suppressed, missing, or flagged cell and what its absence does to the picture.
State what these figures do not capture: benefits, hours, seasonality, part-time work, and the difference between a survey estimate and what an employer will offer next month.
blocks.output: A header line with occupation, SOC, area, and period; a wage table; a Comparison section; a Self-sufficiency section; and a Limitations section.
constraints: Use only the figures supplied. Do not fill a suppressed cell by interpolation or by substituting a statewide number without labeling it.
Attach the reference period to every figure that gets quoted.
Do not convert between hourly and annual without stating the hours assumption you used.
blocks.data: Paste the OEWS rows for this occupation and area, including the statewide row.

prompts.title: Build resume bullets for someone re-entering the workforce
prompts.summary: Finds the skills in a participant's past and unpaid work, supplies action verbs that fit, and handles the time away without apologizing for it.

blocks.role: You are helping a participant who is re-entering the workforce after {{PAST_EXPERIENCE}} and is now aiming for {{TARGET_ROLE}}.
blocks.context: People coming back after time away undersell themselves, describe real work in passive language, and then apologize for the gap in the one document that should be making their case.
steps: List the concrete tasks the participant actually performed, including unpaid work — caregiving, volunteering, informal or family business work — where the participant counts it as experience.
Translate those tasks into the skill language that postings for {{TARGET_ROLE}} actually use.
Give twelve action verbs that fit this work, and list the weak openers to avoid: assisted with, helped, responsible for, duties included.
Draft eight resume bullets. Each leads with a verb, names the scope, and ends with a result. Put a bracketed prompt anywhere only the participant can supply the number.
Recommend how to present the time away — a brief summary line, a skills-forward layout, or nothing at all — and say why that choice fits this case.
Name what an interviewer will ask about the gap and what an honest, unapologetic answer sounds like.
blocks.output: Sections: Tasks performed; Skills in target-role language; Action verbs and what to avoid; Eight draft bullets; Presenting the time away; The gap question.
constraints: Never invent an employer, a date, a credential, or a number.
Do not pad with skills the participant could not demonstrate if asked.
The time away is not a deficiency and the resume should not argue about it.
Keep it to one page unless the participant has more than ten years of relevant history.
blocks.data: Paste what is known about the participant's work history, with names and employers generalized.

prompts.notes: Suggested by Ryan McAlister.

prompts.title: Check a resume against automated screening
prompts.summary: Finds the formatting and keyword problems that keep a resume from being read by a person at all.

blocks.role: You check whether a resume will survive the software an employer uses to parse applications before a human sees it.
blocks.context: Parsers vary and none of them publish their rules. The reliable advice is about structure that is hard to misread, not about tricks.
steps: Flag formatting that parses badly: text in tables, multiple columns, text boxes, graphics, icons, and anything in a header or footer.
Check that the target job title appears in the resume in a form a search would match.
Compare the resume against the posting for terms that are true of the participant and missing from the document.
Check consistency in date formats, job title placement, and section headings, and confirm the contact block sits in the body rather than the header.
Check the file name and the file format against whatever the posting actually asks for.
Give the fix list ordered by how much each one matters.
blocks.output: Sections: Parsing risks; Title and terms; Consistency; File; Fix list in priority order.
constraints: No keyword stuffing, white text, or any other trick. It gets caught and it ends the application.
Do not claim to know a specific employer's system or its rules.
Follow the posting's stated file format instructions over any general advice.
blocks.data: Paste the posting and the resume, with contact details removed.

prompts.title: Coach a participant through the first 90 days of a new job
prompts.summary: Practical workplace success tips, a way to read an unfamiliar culture, and check-in points before a placement quietly falls apart.

blocks.role: You are supporting a participant who just started as {{JOB_TITLE}} and is anxious about {{CONCERN}}.
blocks.context: Most placements that fail do not fail on the work. They fail on the things nobody explains: how questions get asked, when it is acceptable to leave, who to go to when something goes wrong, and how to get through the first month before the first full paycheck.
steps: Give practical things to do in the first two weeks: what to observe, what to write down, who to ask what, and how to ask for clarification without looking lost.

Explain how to read a workplace culture through observable things — how people take breaks, how questions get raised, how direct feedback is, what people wear, when the room goes quiet — rather than through how welcome they feel.
Address the specific concern directly, with two or three things the participant can actually do this week.
Build a check-in schedule at 30, 60, and 90 days, with three questions for each that surface a problem before it becomes a resignation.
List the early warning signs that a placement is at risk — hours changing, being left out of the schedule, a first write-up, transportation breaking down — and what staff should do at each.
Name the supportive services most often needed in the first month, including transportation, uniforms or tools, and the gap before the first paycheck.
blocks.output: Sections: First two weeks; Reading the culture; The specific concern; 30/60/90 check-ins with questions; Warning signs and staff response; Likely supportive service needs.
constraints: Practical and specific. No pep talk, no affirmations.
Do not advise on wage disputes, discrimination, or discipline. Those go to the appropriate authority, and staff should say so plainly.
Do not promise how the employer will behave.
Do not contact the employer, or suggest contacting them, without the participant agreeing to it first.

prompts.title: Collect and shape a participant story ethically
prompts.summary: Plans a story interview, the consent it needs, and the draft that comes out of it, with the participant's dignity and privacy treated as constraints rather than afterthoughts.

blocks.role: Act as a storytelling coordinator for {{ORGANIZATION}} who gathers participant stories ethically and turns them into content, and who has seen what happens when a story outlives the participant's comfort with it.
blocks.context: The story should illustrate {{STORY_PURPOSE}}. A participant story from a workforce program is a story about someone's work history, income, and often a hard year. The person has to be able to say no, change their mind later, and see the draft before anyone else does. The program's confidentiality obligations do not end because the participant said yes.
steps: Write ten interview questions that draw out a before, a turning point, and an after, in the participant's own terms, without leading toward a particular answer or toward a portrait of helplessness.

Build the consent checklist: exactly what they are agreeing to, each place it will appear, how long it will stay up, whether their name and photo are included, that they can withdraw, and how they do that in practice.

List the details that must be removed or generalized before anything is drafted — employer name unless cleared, health, family, legal, or financial specifics, anything that would let a coworker identify them.

If I provided notes or a transcript, draft a 150-word story and three social-length versions, using only quotes that appear in my notes, with the participant's own effort and choices carrying the story.
Mark every sentence in the draft that the participant must approve, and every sentence that would need a second consent because it reveals something the original conversation did not cover.
Give the review process: the participant sees it first, then staff, then it publishes; and the check that has to happen before it is reused in a new place later.
Say plainly whether this story should be told at all right now, and why, if the notes suggest the person is not ready or the risk to them outweighs the value to us.
blocks.output: Sections: Interview questions; Consent checklist; Details to remove or change; Story draft with the social versions, if notes were provided; Sentences requiring approval; Review process; and a closing line titled Should we tell this story now.
constraints: Never invent or embellish a quote. If my notes do not support a sentence, leave it out.
Do not name the participant, their employer, or anyone else in a draft until consent for that specific use is on file.
Do not frame the participant as rescued. The story is about what they did.
Do not include health, family, immigration, legal, or financial details even if the participant offered them, unless they are the point of the story and consent covers them explicitly.
This produces the plan and the draft. The participant's signed release and a staff review are still required before anything is published.
blocks.data: Paste who you plan to interview and their connection to the program (no names yet), where the story will be used, the consent process you have, and interview notes or a transcript if you have them.

prompts.notes: Expanded from the original with a should-we-tell-this check, approval marking, and re-consent for reuse. Forbids invented or embellished quotes.

prompts.title: Decide which BLS or Census series answers a question
prompts.summary: Picks the right federal source, geography, and vintage before anyone pulls a number.

blocks.role: You are a research analyst at {{BOARD_NAME}} deciding which federal data source can actually answer a question about {{AREA}} before any data gets pulled.
blocks.context: Most bad labor market briefs come from asking a source a question it cannot answer: using national projections as a local forecast, or reading a county estimate out of a survey that does not support county detail.
steps: Restate the question in measurable terms: what is being counted, for whom, over what geography and period.

List the candidate sources and what each can and cannot support here — OEWS for occupational wages and employment levels, CES for industry employment over time, LAUS for local unemployment, QCEW for covered employment and establishment counts, the Employment Projections program for growth, ACS for population and workforce characteristics, PUMS for custom cross-tabs, County Business Patterns for establishment size, and LEHD or OnTheMap for commuting and worker flows.
Pick the primary source and state the geography level and the most recent vintage that supports it.
State where the data will be suppressed, unreliable, or unavailable at that geography, and what that does to the answer.
Name the specific table, series, or extract to pull, and where it comes from.
Write the caveat sentence that has to travel with the figure wherever it gets quoted.
blocks.output: Sections: The question, restated; Candidate sources as a table of Source, Answers, Does not answer; Recommendation with geography and vintage; Limitations; What to pull; Required caveat.
constraints: Do not report a number. This produces the plan, not the answer.
If no public source supports the question at this geography, say so and name the closest proxy along with what it costs in accuracy.
Where a survey estimate carries a margin of error large enough to make a comparison meaningless, say that before anyone builds a chart on it.

prompts.title: Design a client intake workflow
prompts.summary: Designing a client intake workflow that is quick, humane, and compliant.

blocks.role: Act as a program operations designer who builds intake processes for social service and workforce programs.
steps: Ask for the hardest-to-obtain documents as late as possible.
blocks.output:
Output format:
1. A step-by-step flow: Step | Who does it | What is collected | Where it is recorded | Target time
2. A document checklist with an alternative accepted document for each, where one exists
3. The decision points where someone can be found ineligible, and the referral to make at each one
4. A field-by-field list of what to collect, each marked Required-for-eligibility, Required-for-reporting, or Nice-to-have — and delete the third category
5. Three ways this process will feel to someone arriving in crisis, and one change for each

prompts.title: Draft a cover letter that is not the resume in paragraphs
prompts.summary: Writes a short letter built on why this job, one piece of proof, and one honest concern addressed.

blocks.role: You draft cover letters that a hiring manager will read to the end, which means under 300 words and no restatement of the resume.
blocks.context: A cover letter earns its place by answering why this job and this employer, and by handling the one thing on the resume that would otherwise raise an eyebrow.
steps: Identify from the posting what problem the employer is trying to solve with this hire.
Open with why this job and this employer specifically, using something concrete from the posting rather than flattery.
Write one paragraph of proof: a single example from the participant's experience, with what they did and what came of it.
Address one likely concern — an employment gap, a career change, a missing credential — plainly and without apology, in two sentences.
Close with a specific next step and a clean sign-off.
Give a shorter variant for an online form with a character limit.
blocks.output: The letter in full, then the short variant, then a note listing anything the participant needs to supply.
constraints: No invented achievements, dates, or numbers. Use bracketed prompts where a fact is missing.
Plain language at about an eighth-grade reading level.
Do not open with "I am writing to apply for" or close with "Thank you for your time and consideration".
Do not apologize for a gap or a career change.
blocks.data: Paste the posting and the relevant experience, with identifying details removed.

prompts.title: Draft a funder progress report
prompts.summary: Turning raw program data into a funder progress report.

prompts.title: Draft a grant statement of need
prompts.summary: Drafting the statement of need section of a grant application.

blocks.role: You are the grant writer at {{BOARD_NAME}}, writing for workforce development funding (federal, state, and foundation programs that serve job seekers and employers in the local area).

prompts.title: Draft a press release
prompts.summary: Produces a release in inverted-pyramid news format, with quote approvals, funder acknowledgments, and a distribution plan handled before it goes out.

blocks.role: Act as a communications officer for {{ORGANIZATION}} who writes press releases in standard news format and has had releases pulled at the last minute because a quote was never approved or a funder was never credited.
blocks.context: A workforce board release usually carries obligations a corporate one does not: funder acknowledgment language, an equal opportunity statement where a program is being promoted, and quotes from board members, elected officials, or partner executives who each have their own approval process. The release is also read by reporters who will call the participant or employer it names, so nothing goes in that has not been cleared.
steps: Identify the single most newsworthy fact and state it in the first sentence with who, what, when, and where. Everything after it is supporting detail in descending order of importance.
Write the body in third person, 350 to 450 words, with no superlative the supplied facts cannot support and no acronym unexplained on first use.
Place quotes after the second paragraph. Use only the approved quotes I supplied. If I wrote NEED DRAFTS, draft one per named speaker and label each one Draft quote — for speaker approval.

Insert every required acknowledgment: funder language, program attribution, and the equal opportunity statement if the release promotes a service. Quote the required wording verbatim where I supplied it.
Build an approvals checklist naming each person or office that must sign off before release, including every quoted speaker, and the order they should be routed in.

Draft the distribution plan: the outlets and beats this fits, the best send time given the embargo, the subject line for the email carrying it, and a two-sentence pitch note for the top three reporters.
List everything in the release a reporter is likely to ask about that we have not yet confirmed we can answer — a participant's availability, an employer's willingness to be named, a figure's source.
blocks.output: A release line reading For immediate release or the embargo date; a headline under 100 characters and a one-sentence subheadline; a dateline and body; quotes after the second paragraph; boilerplate, media contact, and the ### end mark. Then three separate sections: Approvals checklist, Distribution plan, and Before this goes out.
constraints: Never present a drafted quote as something a person actually said.
Do not name a participant, a client, or an employer who has not agreed in writing to be named. Use a bracketed placeholder and add it to the Before this goes out list.
No superlatives the facts cannot support, and no statistic without the source I supplied.
Do not invent a funder acknowledgment or an equal opportunity statement. If I did not supply the wording, leave a marked placeholder and flag it.
blocks.data: Paste the announcement details, approved quotes with speaker names and titles (or write NEED DRAFTS), supporting facts with sources, our boilerplate, the media contact, and any required acknowledgment wording.

prompts.notes: Expanded from the original with approvals routing, a distribution plan, and a pre-release check. Drafted quotes are always labeled for speaker approval and never presented as real statements.

prompts.title: Draft a program year performance narrative
prompts.summary: Builds a narrative around performance results that explains variance honestly and ties it to actions already underway.

Identify the one indicator most at risk next year and say what the board is doing about it now.
Keep each indicator to under 150 words.

prompts.summary: Writing the program design section so the activities connect to the outcomes.

steps: If an activity leads nowhere, or an outcome has no activity producing it, say so.

prompts.title: Test national projections against local conditions
prompts.summary: Stress-tests a projected growth figure against what is actually true about the regional economy.

blocks.role: You are checking whether a national or statewide occupational projection holds up in {{AREA}} before the board plans training capacity around it.

Name the indicators to watch that would tell us early if the projection is wrong.

The rules that govern this check: the WIOA Title I Eligibility Technical Assistance Guide and its Acceptable Documentation List (WSD24-04, September 26, 2024), which require the Local Area to have written local definitions that frontline staff actually follow; source documentation by data element (WSD22-15, June 27, 2023), where a case note must show the participant's status, the date it was obtained, and the staff member who obtained it, and self-attestation is a fallback for items that are unverifiable or unreasonably difficult to obtain, not a default; Selective Service (WSD16-18) for males born on or after January 1, 1960; and authorization to work (WSD18-03, revised September 3, 2024), which must be verified before a job referral, postsecondary education or training, work-based learning such as OJT, or any supportive service that is a direct financial benefit, and need not be photocopied when the document title and expiration date are noted. Local guidance that does not reflect federal and state requirements can produce disallowed costs. Local eligibility policy: {{LOCAL_POLICY_NOTES}}

Check Selective Service status if the applicant is male and was born on or after January 1, 1960, and whether the documentation shows registration, exemption, or a pending determination.
Check whether the services planned in the first 30 days require verified authorization to work before they start.

Where the acceptable documentation list is not pasted, say which items you could not confirm rather than guessing what the list allows.
Do not decide eligibility. Staff make the determination; you identify gaps.
If federal guidance issued after these directives changes a verification rule, flag the conflict and do not resolve it yourself.

prompts.title: Work a low-income determination
prompts.summary: Walks through the WIOA low-income test for one household using the current LLSIL and poverty tables, and shows the arithmetic a monitor will check.

blocks.role: You are an eligibility specialist at {{BOARD_NAME}} working a low-income determination for a {{PROGRAM}} applicant.
blocks.context: Under WSD24-02 (August 20, 2024), an individual is low-income if family income does not exceed the higher of the HHS poverty guideline or 70 percent of the Lower Living Standard Income Level (LLSIL) for the family size. Staff select the LLSIL column for the Local Area's metropolitan statistical area; where a Local Area includes both West: Metro and West: Non-Metro areas, the state uses the higher LLSIL figure for the whole area. Current figures are on EDD's Federal LLSIL and Poverty Guidelines webpage, updated annually. Under WSD24-06, an individual is also low-income if they or their family receive, or in the past six months received, SNAP, TANF, SSI, or state or local income-based public assistance; if they are homeless; or if they have a disability and their own income meets the test even when the family's does not. For Youth (WSD17-07): free or reduced-price lunch eligibility can qualify, living in a high-poverty area (a census tract or county with at least 25 percent poverty) qualifies automatically, UI and child support count as income, and an in-school youth with a disability is assessed on their own income. The income period the Local Area uses is set in local policy: {{INCOME_PERIOD}}.
steps: Check first whether a categorical route (public assistance in the past six months, homelessness, high-poverty area for youth, free or reduced lunch for youth) settles the question without an income calculation, and say which documentation would support it.
If income must be calculated, define the family for this household and state who is included and why.
List each income source, whether it counts, and the annualized amount for the income period, showing the arithmetic.
Look up the higher of the poverty guideline and 70 percent LLSIL for the family size from the pasted table and compare.
If the applicant has a disability, run the individual-income test separately.
State the result, the margin, and what document would need to be in the file to support each figure.
blocks.output: A worked calculation: family composition, an income table (source, counts yes/no, period amount, annualized), the threshold used with its source and year, the comparison, and a one-line result. End with a list of supporting documents to collect.
constraints: Use only the LLSIL and poverty figures pasted below. If none are pasted, stop after the income calculation and say which table is needed.
Do not round in the applicant's favor or against it; show exact figures.
Flag any income source whose treatment is unclear instead of choosing one.
blocks.data: Paste the current California LLSIL and poverty guideline table for your area, and a de-identified list of household members (relationship and age only) and income sources with amounts and pay frequency.

placeholders.label: Income period in local policy
placeholders.default: the six months before application, annualized

prompts.title: Place an Adult applicant in the priority of service order
prompts.summary: Sorts an Adult applicant into the five-tier priority order and lists the documents that prove it, before any individualized or training service is approved.

blocks.role: You are a career services supervisor at {{BOARD_NAME}} confirming an Adult applicant's priority of service category before individualized career or training services are approved.
blocks.context: WSD24-06 (November 8, 2024) requires that WIOA Adult individualized career services and training services go first to recipients of public assistance, other low-income individuals, and individuals who are basic skills deficient (including English language learners), regardless of how much money the Local Area has. It does not apply to basic career services or to the Dislocated Worker program. Status is set at eligibility determination and does not change during participation. The order is: (1) veterans and eligible spouses who are also public assistance recipients, low-income, or basic skills deficient; (2) other public assistance recipients, low-income, or basic skills deficient individuals; (3) veterans and eligible spouses not in those groups; (4) priority populations set by the Governor or the Local Board; (5) everyone else. Basic skills deficient includes: no diploma or equivalent and not enrolled in postsecondary education; enrolled in Title II adult education; skills at or below 8.9 grade level; limited English skills documented by staff observation; or other objective local criteria. The state rate is exiters who were in a priority group and received an individualized or training service, divided by all exiters who received one; Local Areas should strive for 75 percent. Local Board priority populations: {{LOCAL_PRIORITY_GROUPS}}
steps: Determine whether the applicant is a covered person for veterans priority (WSD24-15 uses a broader veteran definition than JVSG: one day of active service, discharged other than dishonorably).
Test each WIOA priority criterion in turn (public assistance, low-income, basic skills deficient) and note which facts support it.
Assign the tier and state the reasoning in two sentences.
List the documentation from WSD24-06's acceptable documentation table that would support the tier, and what to record in the case note.
If the applicant falls in tier 4 or 5, say what that means for the services that can be approved now under local policy.
blocks.output: Tier assigned (1 to 5) with a two-sentence rationale, a checklist of supporting documents, and draft case note text of three to five sentences.
constraints: Do not apply priority of service to basic career services or to a Dislocated Worker enrollment.
Do not move an applicant between tiers based on circumstances that changed after the eligibility determination.
Name a document type only if it appears in WSD24-06's table or in the pasted local policy.
blocks.data: Paste a de-identified summary of the applicant's circumstances: veteran or spouse status, public assistance history, household income result, education level, assessment scores, and English proficiency notes.

placeholders.default: None adopted beyond WIOA priority groups

prompts.title: Audit every point of entry for veterans priority of service
prompts.summary: Walks each way people reach your services and checks whether veterans and eligible spouses are identified, told about priority, and served first.

blocks.role: You are reviewing {{BOARD_NAME}}'s veterans priority of service procedures ahead of the state's annual monitoring.
blocks.context: WSD24-15 (February 14, 2025) applies to every program funded in whole or in part by DOL. Local Boards must have written policies and procedures, keep written copies at every service delivery entry point, display Priority of Service signage where people physically enter, and include priority of service language in contracts, subgrants, solicitations, and MOUs because the requirement cannot be waived. A point of entry is anywhere a veteran or eligible spouse expresses interest in services: reception, resource rooms, kiosks, bulletin boards, CalJOBS, other websites, and the phone, including points run by subrecipients. Identification methods the directive names include asking everyone, regardless of gender, whether they or their spouse are serving or have ever served; looking for VETERAN on a driver's license or ID; kiosk self-identification; and the CalJOBS military service section and flag. Covered persons must be told about their entitlement, the full array of services, and any eligibility requirements. The priority of service definition of veteran (one day of active service, discharged other than dishonorably) is broader than the JVSG and Wagner-Peyser reporting definition (more than 180 days). Eligible spouse categories are limited to the four in the directive.
steps: List every point of entry described below and add any the directive names that are missing from the list.

For each, check identification, notification, signage, written policy availability, and how priority is actually given (earlier in time, or instead of a non-covered person when resources are limited).
Check whether subrecipient points of entry are covered and how the board monitors them.
Check contracts, solicitations, and MOUs for priority of service language.
Check whether staff training uses the correct, broader priority of service veteran definition and the four eligible spouse categories.
Draft the specific procedure language needed to close each gap.
blocks.output: A gap table: Point of entry, Identify, Notify, Signage, Written policy on hand, Gap, Fix. Then draft procedure language for each fix, and a short list of documents a monitor will ask for.
constraints: Treat anything not described below as unknown, not as compliant.
Do not confuse priority of service eligibility with JVSG eligibility for DVOP or LVER services.
Keep fixes to procedures and wording; do not recommend staffing changes.
blocks.data: Describe each point of entry (front desk, phones, website, CalJOBS, youth provider sites, partner sites) and paste your current priority of service policy and the clause your contracts use.

prompts.title: Document a Selective Service knowing-and-willful determination
prompts.summary: Organizes the evidence for an applicant over 25 who did not register, applies the directive's model questions, and drafts the determination memo for the file.

blocks.role: You are an eligibility supervisor at {{BOARD_NAME}} preparing a determination on whether an applicant's failure to register with Selective Service was knowing and willful.
blocks.context: WSD16-18 (April 10, 2017) applies to all WIOA Title I services, not Wagner-Peyser. Males born on or after January 1, 1960, must register between 18 and their 26th birthday. Exemptions include full-time active duty, service academy attendance, continuous confinement to a residence or institution due to disability, confinement during the window (with registration due within 30 days of release if still under 26), veterans discharged after their 26th birthday, non-citizens who first entered after their 26th birthday or are on a valid non-immigrant visa. An applicant 26 or older who was required to register and did not may be served only if the failure was not knowing and willful. The entity that enrolls the applicant makes that determination; the local policy decides whether a Status Information Letter is requested first. Evidence can include a DD-214 showing honorable service, third-party affidavits, and the applicant's own signed statement, which may be enough when other evidence is unavailable. The directive's model questions ask whether the applicant knew of the requirement, was misinformed, when they first learned, where they lived from 18 to 26, whether Selective Service letters went unanswered, whether the failure was deliberate, whether they had the capacity to choose, and what they did on learning of it. If services are denied, the applicant must be told about the grievance procedure, and the evidence must be kept. Local policy on Status Information Letters: {{SIL_POLICY}}
steps: Confirm from the facts that registration was required, or identify the exemption that applies and stop there.
Organize the evidence by source (documents, third parties, applicant statement) and note dates covered.
Answer each model question for 'knowing' and each for 'willful' from the evidence, marking any answered only by the applicant's statement.
State the recommended determination and the evidence that carries it.
Draft the determination memo for the file and, if the recommendation is denial, the notice to the applicant with grievance rights.
blocks.output: An exemption check, an evidence table, a model-question table (question, answer, source), a recommended determination, and a draft memo of no more than one page. Add the denial notice only if the recommendation is denial.
constraints: Make a recommendation, not a final determination; the authorized staff member decides.
Do not treat a missing Status Information Letter as proof of a knowing and willful failure.
Use neutral language; do not characterize the applicant's motives beyond what the evidence shows.
blocks.data: Paste a de-identified summary: birth year, citizenship or entry timing, where the applicant lived from 18 to 26, military service, any confinement periods with dates, the Status Information Letter result if any, and the applicant's written explanation.

Decide without first requesting a Status Information Letter

prompts.title: Determine in-school or out-of-school youth eligibility
prompts.summary: Works a youth applicant through the ISY or OSY criteria, the low-income rules, and the five percent caps that a single file can quietly break.

blocks.role: You are a youth program eligibility reviewer at {{BOARD_NAME}} determining whether an applicant qualifies as an out-of-school or in-school youth.
blocks.context: Under WSD17-07 (January 16, 2018): an out-of-school youth (OSY) is 16 to 24, not attending secondary or postsecondary school (Title II adult education, YouthBuild, Job Corps, high school equivalency programs, non-credit postsecondary classes, dropout re-engagement, and certain charter schools do not count as school), and has at least one barrier: dropout; within compulsory age but missed the most recent complete school quarter; diploma holder who is low-income and basic skills deficient or an English language learner; offender; homeless or runaway; foster care or aged out; pregnant or parenting; disability; or low-income and requires additional assistance. An in-school youth (ISY) is 14 to 21 (22 with an IEP), attending school, low-income, and has at least one barrier from the ISY list. Eligibility is fixed at intake and does not change until exit. No more than five percent of ISY enrolled in a program year may qualify solely on 'requires additional assistance,' and the five percent low-income exception covers youth who would otherwise need to be low-income. For income: free or reduced lunch can qualify; living in a census tract or county with at least 25 percent poverty qualifies automatically; UI and child support count as income; an ISY with a disability is assessed on their own income. The Local Board defines 'requires additional assistance': {{RAA_DEFINITION}}. Current program-year counts toward the five percent limits: {{FIVE_PERCENT_COUNTS}}.
steps: Decide school status at intake using the directive's exclusions, and state ISY or OSY.
Check age against the category's range.
Test each barrier on the relevant list and identify every one the facts support, not just the first.
Determine whether low-income status is required for this applicant's category and barrier, and if so whether a categorical route applies.
If eligibility rests on 'requires additional assistance' or the low-income exception, check the five percent counts and say whether this enrollment fits.
List the documentation needed for each criterion relied on.
blocks.output: A determination summary (ISY or OSY, eligible or not, criteria relied on), a barrier table with documentation for each, a five percent check, and any open questions staff must resolve before enrollment.
constraints: Rely on the barrier that is best documented, and record the others as additional barriers.
Do not reclassify a youth later because their school status or age changed after intake.
If the Local Board is using the OSY expenditure waiver in WSD25-04, note that it changes the spending requirement, not the eligibility rules.
blocks.data: Paste a de-identified summary: age, school enrollment status and type, last attendance, diploma status, household and income facts, and any barrier information with how it would be documented.

prompts.title: Write a CalJOBS case note that will pass data validation
prompts.summary: Turns a staff member's rough account of a contact into a case note that records status, date, and who obtained it, and names the activity it supports.

blocks.role: You write CalJOBS case notes for {{BOARD_NAME}} career coaches. A state validator, not the coach, is the reader who matters.
blocks.context: WSD22-15 defines a case note as a statement by the case manager that identifies, at minimum, the participant's status for a specific data element, the date the information was obtained, and the staff member who obtained it. During Data Element Validation (WSD24-16), a reported value with no allowable source document is scored 'unable to validate,' which counts as an error just like a mismatch. WSD24-05 requires data entry within 30 days of the activity, detailed case notes documenting progress in training, and a check with the training provider at least quarterly (monthly preferred). Stipends and incentive payments need a case note that states the justification, the contribution to the participant's success, and how the amount was calculated (WSD23-08). Follow-up services must be more than a contact attempt.
steps: Identify every data element or service the contact establishes or changes, and the activity it belongs to.
Write the case note in plain past tense: what was verified or provided, how it was verified, the date, and the staff member.
For any status established by participant statement, say so explicitly rather than implying it was verified.
List the source document that should be uploaded to support each element, if one exists.
Flag anything in the rough notes that does not belong in a case note: opinions about the person, health details beyond what the element requires, or third parties' information.
blocks.output: The case note text, ready to paste, followed by a short table of Data element or service, Source document to upload, and a list of anything removed and why.
constraints: Keep it factual. No adjectives about the participant's attitude or character.
Do not invent dates, document names, or staff names; leave a bracketed blank where something is missing.
Keep each note under 150 words unless it documents a stipend, incentive, or training progress.
blocks.data: Paste the coach's rough notes with names, IDs, and dates of birth removed.

prompts.notes: Grounded in WSD22-15, WSD24-05, WSD24-16, and WSD23-08.

prompts.title: Sort a participant's services into CalJOBS categories before entry
prompts.summary: Classifies each planned or delivered service by WSD24-05 service type, its effect on participation and the exit clock, and the entry rule that most often goes wrong.

blocks.role: You are a CalJOBS data quality lead at {{BOARD_NAME}} helping a coach enter a participant's services correctly the first time.
blocks.context: WSD24-05 (October 10, 2024) requires entry within 30 days of the activity. Self-service basic career services do not extend the exit date; staff-assisted basic, individualized career, training, and youth services do. Supportive services (other than youth services) and follow-up services do not extend exit, and a supportive service code can only be added while a qualifying service code is open. For Youth, Objective Assessment (412) and Development of Individual Employment Plan (413) must come before other youth services and do not themselves create participation; OJT for youth is work experience, not training. For Adult and Dislocated Worker, a training activity code is entered only when a program in common exit pays some of the cost through an ITA or an authorized training contract (OJT, customized, incumbent worker, Local Board determination training); training paid entirely by an outside source is recorded as 313 (Placed in State and Local Training), optionally tracked with 315, which places the participant in neither the credential nor the MSG measure. Do not open a new training code for gaps between terms of the same program. Co-funded services get one activity code, not duplicates. Under WSD24-07, a participant exits after 90 consecutive days with no services and none scheduled, applied retroactively to the last service date. The activity code list itself is an attachment to WSD24-05: {{CODE_LIST_STATUS}}.
steps: List each service with its date and funding source.
Assign each a service type (self-service basic, staff-assisted basic, individualized career, training, youth program element, supportive, follow-up, housekeeping).
For each, state whether it creates participation, extends the exit date, and whether it requires an open qualifying code or verified work authorization first.
Apply the training-code rules and say whether a training code, 313, or 315 is correct.
Project the exit date that will result if nothing else is scheduled, and flag any service that will be lost to a system-closed status if not entered within 30 days.
Where the code list is pasted, suggest the specific code; otherwise name the category and leave the code blank.
blocks.output: A table: Service, Date, Funding, Service type, Creates participation, Extends exit, Prerequisite, Suggested code. Then the projected exit date and a short list of entry warnings.
constraints: Never suggest a code number that is not in the pasted list.
Do not enter a training code to make a participant count in a measure when the funding rule does not support it.
Flag supportive services that are being used to keep a case open; they do not extend exit.
blocks.data: Paste a de-identified list of services provided or planned, with dates, who paid, and how (ITA, contract, other source). Paste the WSD24-05 activity code list if you have it.

prompts.title: Draft a stipend and incentive payment policy
prompts.summary: Builds the local policy WSD23-08 requires before any stipend or incentive is paid, with the six required elements and the documentation rules.

blocks.role: You are drafting {{BOARD_NAME}}'s stipend and incentive payment policy for {{PROGRAMS}}.
blocks.context: WSD23-08 (May 23, 2024) applies to WIOA formula, discretionary, and state general funds. A policy must be in place before any payment. Stipends are fixed payments for participation in activities requiring a substantial or regular time commitment; incentive payments recognize achievement tied to work experience, education, training, employment, or other activities. Neither may be paid in lieu of wages; where wages are the right payment, wages must be paid under work-based learning policy. The policy must (a) justify how payments align with program goals, who is served, and why they are needed; (b) align with organizational policy; (c) follow 2 CFR 200.438 (no entertainment), which the directive also applies to state funds; (d) ensure payments are not used in lieu of wages; (e) set the method for determining need and amounts and how determinations are documented; and (f) distinguish stipends from incentives if both are used. Every payment needs a case note with the justification, its contribution to success, and how the amount was calculated and why it is reasonable. Participation or achievement must be verified before payment. Activity codes named in the directive: Adult stipends 197, Youth stipends 494, Adult incentives 183, Youth incentives 419. Entities must decide whether payments are taxable and must tell participants they may affect public benefits, referring them to the benefits agency or a certified benefits planner. Local constraints: {{LOCAL_CONSTRAINTS}}
steps: Draft a purpose and scope section naming the funding streams and programs covered.
Write definitions that keep stipends, incentives, and wages clearly apart, with one example of each and one example of a payment that must be a wage.
Write each required element (a) through (f) as a numbered policy section.
Set out an amount schedule structure with placeholders and the method for setting amounts, without inventing dollar figures.
Write the documentation and verification procedure, including the case note elements, the activity codes, and the fiscal records that prove payment and receipt.
Write the participant notice language on taxes and public benefits.
List the approvals needed before the policy takes effect.
blocks.output: A policy draft with numbered sections, a blank amount schedule table, a one-paragraph participant notice, and a compliance checklist mapping each WSD23-08 requirement to the section that meets it.
constraints: Do not set dollar amounts; leave bracketed blanks for the board to decide.
Do not give tax advice. Say the organization must determine taxability with its own advisor.
Confirm activity codes against the current WSD24-05 code list before publishing.

prompts.title: Plan strategic co-enrollment for a participant
prompts.summary: Maps which partner programs a participant could be co-enrolled in, who pays for what, and how the shared case is managed without duplicate services.

blocks.role: You are a career coach at {{BOARD_NAME}} building a co-enrollment plan for a participant who could benefit from more than one Unified Plan partner program.
blocks.context: WSD19-09 (February 12, 2020) strongly encourages strategic co-enrollment: deliberate enrollment in more than one Unified Plan partner program to share case management, leverage resources, and avoid duplication or supplanting. In CalJOBS (WSD24-05), a co-funded service gets one activity code, not one per funding stream; the participant must already be a participant in each funding stream that co-funds a service. Common exit (WSD24-07) means services from any DOL program in common exit, including Title I, Wagner-Peyser, JVSG, NDWG, and TAA, keep the exit date open. Show how the training and supportive costs would be split so no cost is paid twice.
Note CalJOBS entry implications: which programs enroll first and how co-funded activities are recorded.
List the referral steps in order with owners.

prompts.title: Route a complaint to the right process
prompts.summary: Decides whether a complaint is a WIOA grievance, a discrimination complaint, an Employment Service complaint, or an incident report, and lays out the clock that starts today.

blocks.role: You are the compliance lead at {{BOARD_NAME}} deciding which complaint process applies to something a participant, employer, or staff member has raised.
blocks.context: Four separate processes exist, and choosing the wrong one loses deadlines. (1) WIOA Title I grievances (WSD18-05): noncriminal programmatic violations; must be filed in writing within one year of the alleged violation; the filing date is the date any Local Area office, AJCC partner, provider, or subrecipient receives it; the Local Area must offer informal resolution, hold a hearing within 30 days of filing with at least 10 days' notice, and issue a written decision within 60 days; an adverse decision can be appealed to the state within 10 days of receipt, and a request for EDD review may be filed within 15 days when no decision arrives or reprisal occurs. Displacement complaints from regular employees also go through this process (WSD19-02). (2) Discrimination complaints under WIOA Section 188 (WSD17-01): filed within 180 days with the Local Area EO Officer or directly with DOL's Civil Rights Center; the EO Officer issues a written acknowledgment with notice of the right to representation, offers alternative dispute resolution, and has 90 days to issue a Notice of Final Action; the complainant may then go to the Civil Rights Center within 30 days. (3) Employment Service complaints (WSD23-09): complaints about ES regulations, such as a CalJOBS job order or EDD staff, or about employment-related law such as wages, hours, health and safety, or trafficking, are taken by EDD Complaint Representatives at AJCCs; UI and Disability Insurance complaints are not part of this system. (4) Criminal fraud, waste, abuse, or misconduct (WSD24-03): reported to DOL's Office of Inspector General, not handled as a grievance. Local EO Officer: {{EO_OFFICER}}. Local grievance contact: {{GRIEVANCE_CONTACT}}.
steps: Summarize what is alleged, against whom, and when it happened, in three sentences.
Decide which process or processes apply and explain why. A single complaint can trigger more than one.
Calculate the filing deadline for each applicable process from the date of the alleged event, and say whether it has passed.
List what must happen in the next 10 days: acknowledgment, forwarding, logging, notice to the respondent, informal resolution offer.
Draft the acknowledgment to the complainant in plain language at a sixth-grade reading level, including how to get language assistance and auxiliary aids.
Note any immediate protective step: separating the complainant from the respondent, preserving records, or contacting law enforcement if someone is in danger.
blocks.output: A routing decision table (Process, Applies yes/no, Why, Deadline, Who handles), a 10-day action list with owners, and the draft acknowledgment letter.
constraints: Do not decide the merits of the complaint.
Do not discourage filing or suggest the complaint is untimely without stating the exact deadline and the source.
Treat reprisal against a complainant as its own issue to escalate.
If an allegation might be criminal, route it to incident reporting even if it is also a grievance.
blocks.data: Paste a de-identified description of the complaint: what happened, when, who is involved by role, how and when it was received, and anything already done.

prompts.notes: Grounded in WSD18-05, WSD17-01, WSD23-09, WSD24-03, and WSD19-02. Days in WSD18-05 are consecutive calendar days.

prompts.title: Decide whether something must be incident-reported, and draft it
prompts.summary: Tests a concern against the incident categories in WSD24-03, sets the reporting clock, and drafts the report and the internal record.

blocks.role: You are the designated incident reporting contact at {{BOARD_NAME}} assessing a concern that may need to go to the Department of Labor's Office of Inspector General.
blocks.context: WSD24-03 (September 17, 2024) requires each subrecipient to have written incident reporting procedures and a designated staff person. Reportable categories include fraud, misfeasance, nonfeasance, or malfeasance (bribery, forgery, embezzlement, theft of participant checks, kickbacks, payments to fake enrollees, misrepresenting official reports); misapplication of funds where intent appears (nepotism, political patronage, ineligible enrollees, conflicts of interest, using funds for other than specified purposes), not minor mismanagement; gross mismanagement (unauditable records, unsupported costs, highly inaccurate reports, payroll deductions not paid to the IRS, lack of internal controls); and employee or participant misconduct. Reports go in two steps: complete the OIG Hotline Portal, then email a copy, including screenshots of the three portal screens, to ETAIncidentReporting@dol.gov. If internet access is unavailable, the OIG hotlines are 1-800-347-3756 and 1-202-693-6999. Emergencies, meaning imminent health or safety concerns or an imminent loss of more than $50,000, must be reported no later than one working day after discovery. The portal is not for grievances, EEO complaints, labor disputes, or personnel matters. Reporting does not replace the duty to act immediately to prevent further loss, including calling local law enforcement. Complainants may remain anonymous and may report directly to the OIG. Records must be kept at least three years, and longer while any audit, claim, or litigation is open.
steps: Restate the concern in neutral, factual terms without naming individuals.
Test it against each reportable category and say which, if any, it fits, and why.
Decide whether it is an emergency under the directive's definition and state the reporting deadline.
List immediate protective actions: stopping payments, securing records, restricting system access, notifying law enforcement.
Draft the factual narrative for the OIG portal: what, when, where, how discovered, dollar amount if known, program and funding stream.
Draft the internal file memo recording the decision, the date and time reported, and who was notified.
blocks.output: A determination (reportable or not, category, emergency or not, deadline), an immediate action list, a draft portal narrative under 400 words, and a draft internal memo.
constraints: Work from a summary only. Do not paste source records, personnel files, or participant files.
State facts and their source; do not state conclusions about anyone's guilt or intent.
If the concern is a grievance, EEO complaint, or personnel issue, say so and route it there instead.
When unsure whether a matter is reportable, say so and recommend consulting counsel or the Regional Advisor rather than deciding not to report.
blocks.data: Paste a de-identified summary of what was observed or alleged, how it came to light, the dates, the funding involved, and any action already taken.

prompts.notes: Grounded in WSD24-03 (superseded WSD20-12). TEGL 15-23 has the detailed DOL instructions.

prompts.title: Check participant-facing material for EO and language access
prompts.summary: Reviews a flyer, letter, web page, or form for the equal opportunity statement, accessibility contacts, Babel notice, and translation obligations before it goes out.

blocks.role: You are the equal opportunity and language access reviewer for {{BOARD_NAME}} checking a piece before it is printed, posted, or mailed.
blocks.context: WSD17-01 requires that recruitment brochures and other materials describing WIOA Title I programs, in print, electronic, or oral form, state that the program is an 'equal opportunity employer/program' and that 'auxiliary aids and services are available upon request to individuals with disabilities.' Where a voice phone number is listed, a TTY or equally effective option must also appear; the California Relay Service is 711 or 1-800-735-2922. Media publications and broadcasts must carry the same statements. Materials must not suggest, by text or illustration, that anyone is treated differently on a prohibited basis. WSD17-03 requires free, timely language assistance; vital information must be translated into languages spoken by a significant portion of the population eligible to be served or likely to be encountered; communications of vital information must carry a Babel notice explaining how to get language help; once a person's preferred language is known, vital information must be conveyed in that language; and staff may not rely on a person's minor child or on family or friends to interpret except in an emergency, for information of minimal importance, or when the person asks and a record is kept. Threshold languages for this area: {{THRESHOLD_LANGUAGES}}.
steps: Classify the piece: does it describe a WIOA Title I program, and does it contain vital information (eligibility, rights, deadlines, decisions, required actions)?
Check for the exact EO statement and the auxiliary aids statement, and for TTY or relay information next to any phone number.
Check images and wording for anything implying who is or is not welcome.
If the piece carries vital information, check for a Babel notice and decide which threshold-language translations are required.
Check basic accessibility: reading level, contrast described in the draft, alt text for images, and whether the format works with a screen reader.
Produce corrected text.
blocks.output: A checklist (Requirement, Present, Fix), then the corrected text with additions marked, then a one-line list of translations needed.
constraints: Use the directive's exact EO wording; do not paraphrase it.
Do not translate the piece yourself as the final version; mark translations as needing a qualified translator.
Keep the reviewer's changes minimal outside the required elements.
blocks.data: Paste the full text of the piece, and describe any images and where it will be used.

prompts.notes: Grounded in WSD17-01 and WSD17-03. Confirm your threshold languages against your own LEP plan; the default here is only a starting point.

prompts.title: Build a desk guide for recognizing and referring trafficking victims
prompts.summary: Creates a one-page guide for front-desk and career services staff on signs of trafficking, what to say, who to call, and how to keep serving the person.

blocks.role: You are writing a desk guide for {{BOARD_NAME}} AJCC staff on recognizing possible human trafficking and making referrals.
blocks.context: WSD18-09 (January 31, 2019) reminds Local Area staff that many victims do not self-identify, and lists common signs such as not holding one's own identification or travel documents, appearing coached on what to say, and having been recruited for one job and forced into another. Its Attachment 1 has fuller indicators and Attachment 2 lists hotlines. If someone is in immediate danger, staff call 911. Victims who are U.S. citizens or lawful residents receive the same WIOA services as anyone; foreign nationals who are victims of a severe form of trafficking or hold T nonimmigrant status are also eligible for WIOA Title I services, and services follow the same case management processes as other AJCC customers. Under WSD23-09, trafficking allegations involving an employer are also employment-related law complaints that EDD Complaint Representatives at the AJCC can take. Local referral partners: {{LOCAL_PARTNERS}}
steps: Write a short 'what you might notice' list drawn from the directive and its attachment if pasted, phrased as observations rather than conclusions.
Write 'what to do' as a numbered sequence: ensure immediate safety, offer privacy, use a qualified interpreter, avoid interrogating, offer referral.
Write two or three sample sentences staff can say that are calm and non-leading.
List who to call: 911 for immediate danger, the hotlines from Attachment 2, local partners, and the internal contact.
Explain how to continue employment and training services and how eligibility works for T visa holders.
State what goes in the case file and what does not.
blocks.output: A one-page desk guide with headed sections: What you might notice, What to do, What to say, Who to call, Keep serving, What to document.
constraints: Do not tell staff to investigate, confront an employer, or contact immigration authorities.
Use only hotline numbers that appear in the pasted Attachment 2 or that the user supplies; leave blanks otherwise.
Keep language non-stigmatizing and trauma-informed.
blocks.data: Paste WSD18-09 Attachments 1 and 2 if you have them, and your internal escalation contact.

prompts.notes: Grounded in WSD18-09 and WSD23-09. Hotline numbers change; verify them before printing.

prompts.title: Review a work experience or OJT worksite agreement
prompts.summary: Checks a worksite or OJT agreement for displacement protections, wage and benefit obligations, waiver eligibility, and the work experience policy elements before signature.

blocks.role: You are a business services compliance reviewer at {{BOARD_NAME}} checking a {{AGREEMENT_TYPE}} agreement before it is signed.
blocks.context: WSD19-02 (July 11, 2019): a WIOA participant may not displace any currently employed worker, including partial displacement through reduced non-overtime hours, wages, or benefits; may not be placed in a job while anyone is on layoff from the same or a substantially equivalent job; may not fill a vacancy created by terminating a regular employee or reducing the workforce for that purpose; and may not be placed in a promotional line that infringes on current workers' promotion. Where a program conflicts with a collective bargaining agreement, the union and employer must give written concurrence before it begins. Displaced workers can use the WIOA grievance process. WSD15-26 (June 3, 2016): the employer of record for subsidized employment must be checked against the Affordable Care Act and California paid sick leave law; California's sick leave entitlement has been expanded since 2015, so confirm the current Labor Code requirements. WSD17-07: Local Board work experience policy must address duration, hour limits, and incentives and stipends. WSD18-03: verify authorization to work before referring a participant to an employer. WSD25-03 (April 9, 2026): a Local Board approved for the PY 26-27 OJT waiver may reimburse up to 90 percent of wages (instead of the statutory 50 percent) only for businesses with 50 or fewer employees, and must keep records proving employer size. Waiver status for this board: {{WAIVER_STATUS}}.
steps: Identify the employer of record, the position, wage, hours, duration, and reimbursement rate in the agreement.
Check each displacement and promotional-line prohibition and whether the agreement includes an employer certification covering it.
Check for a collective bargaining agreement and, if one exists, the written concurrence.
Check wage, sick leave, and other employer-of-record obligations, and flag where current California law must be confirmed.
For OJT, check the reimbursement rate against the statute and the waiver, and whether employer size is documented.
For work experience, check the agreement against the local work experience policy elements.
List missing clauses and draft language for each.
blocks.output: A review table (Requirement, Agreement section, Met / Missing / Unclear, Fix), draft clause language for each gap, and a sign / revise / do not sign recommendation.
constraints: Do not treat a reimbursement above 50 percent as allowed unless the waiver status confirms approval for this program year and the employer has 50 or fewer employees.
Do not give legal advice on employment law; flag items for counsel.
Quote the agreement's section numbers when citing it.
blocks.data: Paste the agreement text, the employer's headcount and any union information, and your local work experience or OJT policy.

options: Approved for both waivers this program year
Approved for the OJT waiver only
Approved for the transitional jobs waiver only
